children: Efforts to push down long-term U.S. borrowing costs will not address the underlying forces driving yields higher unless policymakers tackle the country's fiscal deficits, according to Howard Marks, co-chair of Oaktree Capital Management.

Marks said Treasury bond purchases could temporarily lower yields but would not resolve the factors behind higher long-term rates. “The goal shouldn’t be to get interest rates down. It should be to respond to the factors pushing rates up,” he wrote in a memo.

Marks identified persistent inflation, large fiscal deficits, Treasury issuance, and strong demand for capital as factors putting upward pressure on borrowing costs. He said the U.S. was running a deficit of about 6% of GDP, while net interest outlays were projected to exceed $1T this year.

“The U.S. displays a total lack of fiscal discipline,” Marks wrote, describing the dollar's reserve-currency status as a “golden credit card” that the U.S. had used unwisely. He argued that large deficits could also add to inflation by boosting liquidity and aggregate demand.

Marks also said Treasury buybacks would not change the government's overall indebtedness if they were accompanied by greater Treasury bill issuance. Instead, such transactions could shorten the maturity of government debt and require more frequent refinancing.

He said the growing need for capital from federal deficits, economic growth, and AI investment was also putting pressure on interest rates. Marks cited McKinsey's estimate that more than $5T would be spent worldwide through 2030 on AI-related data centers and said the Treasury would also need to refinance a large volume of maturing securities while financing annual deficits.

Marks said the longer-term solution was fiscal restraint rather than attempts to suppress borrowing costs. He called for greater fiscal responsibility, higher revenues as a share of GDP through higher income tax rates and the elimination of tax preferences, and slower growth in government spending than GDP.

“The issue at hand isn’t a matter of conjecture . . . just math,” Marks wrote, arguing that the U.S. was spending more than it collected, increasing debt relative to GDP and facing a rapidly growing interest bill.

Despite his concerns over U.S. fiscal management, Marks did not advocate a wholesale move out of dollar assets. He said investors shifting into non-dollar or non-U.S. assets would take on other risks and cautioned that moving money out of the U.S. on a large scale could prove unsuccessful.
Marks said that the U.S. could not “perpetually spend more than it takes in” without eventually raising questions about the creditworthiness of its currency and Treasury securities.
